The 2013 Ebola virus disease (EVD) outbreak in West Africa resulted in over 28,000 cases by December 2015. It is estimated that over 10,000 EVD survivors may require convalescent care. Survivors face a range of shortand long-term medical issues, including mental health challenges for both survivors and their families or communities. Additionally, the persistence of the Ebola virus in certain body compartments, such as semen, raises concerns about the potential reintroduction of the virus in areas where transmission has been previously eliminated. EVD survivors require comprehensive medical and psychosocial support to address their challenges and minimize the risk of continued virus transmission, particularly through sexual transmission. This document provides guidance on clinical care, virus testing, and the planning and delivery of ongoing health services for EVD survivors. The primary audience for this guidance includes healthcare professionals providing primary care to EVD survivors. It may also be used by family or community members supporting survivors, as well as healthcare planners and policymakers. This guidance was developed by WHO with input from stakeholders, including Ministries of Health in Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone, members of the UN Global Ebola Response Coalition, WHO country offices, and other organizations with expertise in EVD survivor care. Due to the limited scientific evidence on clinical care for EVD survivors and the urgent need for guidance, the recommendations are based on expert consensus. The guidance will be reviewed and updated as new evidence emerges. The unprecedented scale of the West African EVD outbreak has provided opportunities to enhance clinical observations and understanding of the health challenges faced by survivors. Findings from high-resource settings in Europe and North America, where detailed investigations are possible, have contributed to this understanding. New presentations and complications of EVD are being discovered regularly, and further findings are anticipated as care capacity for survivors in West Africa grows. WHO will continue to monitor research developments and update recommendations as needed. The guidance will be updated six months after publication unless significant new evidence necessitates earlier revision. Comments and suggestions for additional issues to include in future updates are welcomed. An EVD survivor is defined as a person with a confirmed positive result on RT-PCR testing for Ebola virus in any body fluid who subsequently recovered, or someone who is IgM and/or IgG positive on serological testing for EVD and has not been vaccinated against the virus. These definitions may be adjusted during an epidemic to reflect the local situation. Survivor status is often verified using government or laboratory-issued EVD Survivor’s Certificates, though cross-checking with treatment unit records and antibody testing may be required. An integrated care program is essential to address the medical and psychosocial needs of EVD survivors and reduce the risk of virus reintroduction. Ideally, medical services for survivors should be integrated into existing health services. In areas where such services are unavailable or inaccessible, establishing survivor-specific services may be necessary. The long-term goal should be to strengthen health systems for all individuals and health problems. Before discharge from an Ebola treatment unit (ETU), survivors should receive education and counseling about potential sequelae and psychosocial challenges during recovery. Family members should also be included in discussions about common sequelae, virus transmission risks, and preventive measures. Survivors should be given a follow-up appointment within two weeks of discharge and clear instructions on whom to contact for health concerns. Issues such as confidentiality, stigma, and the cost of follow-up care should be addressed. Survivors with significant mental health issues may require direct referral to mental health providers. At discharge, survivors should be provided with documents containing their unique patient ID, name, age, symptoms at presentation, convalescent symptoms, test results, treatment records, and their EVD Survivor’s Certificate. These documents should be brought to all future clinic or hospital visits. Sexual health education and counseling should be offered to all survivors, with specific guidance for male survivors and their partners regarding virus persistence in semen and transmission prevention. Pregnant survivors should receive counseling on maternal and fetal risks associated with EVD and virus persistence. The first follow-up visit after ETU discharge should include a comprehensive medical history, physical examination, and evaluations of musculoskeletal, ocular, auditory, abdominal, neurological, mental, and sexual health. Social workers should address stigma, economic status, shelter, food security, dependents, and social support. Routine laboratory tests, such as complete blood count and creatinine, should be performed, with additional tests as indicated. Regular follow-up is recommended for at least one year, regardless of symptoms at discharge. Suggested follow-up includes an initial outpatient evaluation within two weeks, monthly visits for six months, and quarterly visits thereafter. Male survivors should coordinate follow-up visits with semen testing. Detailed evaluations should be conducted at least every three months during the first year. Musculoskeletal pain, particularly arthralgia, is one of the most common sequelae, affecting 50-75% of survivors. The pain is typically symmetrical, polyarticular, and worse in the morning or after exercise, often involving large joints. Periarticular tenosynovitis, especially in the shoulders and hips, may occur and is consistent with spondyloarthritis. Physical examination may reveal signs of inflammatory arthritis, such as swelling and tenderness. Costochondritis is also commonly reported. Clinical evaluation should distinguish between non-inflammatory arthralgia and inflammatory arthritis. Radiographs are generally unnecessary unless new deformities are observed. Differential diagnoses for joint and muscle pain include degenerative joint disease, autoimmune diseases, polymyositis, dermatomyositis, and septic arthritis. Treatment options include warm compresses, exercise, addressing psychosocial issues, and first-line therapy with paracetamol.
